newsitem.title: USA: NATO said readying arms proposal.
newsitem.headline: NATO said readying arms proposal.

text.p: The United States and its allies are preparing a conventional arms-reduction proposal that is a major part of their effort to reassure Russia about the non-threatening nature of NATO expansion, officials said on Friday.

Washington had been hoping NATO could agree on the broad outlines of the proposal by early next week. But one official told Reuters that differences -- within the administration and among allies -- likely would delay agreement for another week.
The proposal concerns modifications in the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe treaty, which was negotiated by the two Cold War alliances, NATO and the Warsaw Pact.
It already has caused the United States, Russia and others of the pact's 30 signatories to eliminate more than 58,000 pieces of equipment from their forces in Europe.

Russia has become increasingly vocal in opposing NATO's plan to decide at a July summit which former communist bloc countries will be inducted into the western alliance. Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic are the top contenders.

Moscow has demanded a binding treaty with NATO that would give it an effective veto over important security issues. While the alliance has signalled this will not be possible, it is putting together a package of measures to reassure Moscow.

This is to include assurances on NATO deployments, a formal arrangement for regular consultations, financial aid and a boost to Russia's role in forums like the Group of Seven (G7). NATO has said it has no plans to deploy nuclear weapons in its new member states.
The NATO proposal for further reductions and reconfigurations in Europe-based conventional forces is a major component of this effort, U.S. officials said.

"The Russian concern about the military infrastructure in NATO is about conventional forces in Europe. So there is an opportunity to use this current round of CFE negotiations to address some of Russia's concerns and since CFE is a treaty, it is legally binding," one senior U.S. official told Reuters.

Another official predicted the NATO proposal, once put forward, would contain "significant reductions" in levels of weapons -- armoured personnel carriers, artillery, tanks, combat aircraft and attack helicopters -- permitted under CFE.

A third official said: "We all agreed we want this (proposal) to be one of the avenues for reassuring the Russians about NATO enlargement. But we also have to protect the future military flexibility of the alliance."
He added that developing the allied proposal "has proven to be somewhat more difficult than we anticipated" because of differences within the administration and among the allies.

Officials said the proposed new reductions will affect the United States and Russia -- which currently are allowed more weapons than they have on the ground -- as well as some, but not all, of the other countries who signed the treaty.
They said NATO and Russia have common interest in setting national limits on arms -- rather than the bloc-to-bloc limits now in the treaty.
But Russia wants to cap the number of weapons an alliance can field, something the Americans oppose as discriminatory because NATO is the only military alliance left, they said.

Moscow also wants constraints on forward deployment of conventional forces in new NATO states. One official said: "We're open to the idea of preventing destabilising concentrations (of arms in those states) ... What is unacceptable is an outright prohibition on stationing forces."

Jack Mendelsohn, deputy director of the non-profit Arms Control Association, said Russia's interest in trying to bring dual-capable aircraft -- which can be used for conventional or nuclear purposes -- clearly will not find favour in NATO.

Similarly, Russia almost certainly would oppose NATO efforts to let alliance members swap CFE weapon limits, he said. For instance, the Russians, in time of tension, "don't want an unfettered possibility for German or Turkish forces to be built up at the expense of some (NATO) ally (like Portugal) that everybody knew wouldn't fight anyway," Mendelsohn said.
He said the proposal will be an important opportunity to prove to Russia NATO's "good faith (and) that we're not trying to put them at a more severe military disadvantage."
